bigPicture.subtitle: Light, Love, and the Assurance of Eternal Life
paragraphs: Picture a church in turmoil. A group of its own members — some of them gifted teachers — have walked out. Before they left, they taught that they had a higher knowledge of God; that the eternal Christ could never truly have come in a body of flesh; that what you do with your body does not matter to your spirit; that they had moved beyond sin. Those who stayed are shaken. Were the leavers right? Do we really know God? Are we really saved?

Into that confusion an old man writes a letter. He does not open with his name. He opens with what he has seen and touched: “That which was from the beginning, that which we have heard, that which we have seen with our eyes, that which we saw, and our hands touched, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). He is one of the original eyewitnesses, and he writes to give his ‘little children’ certainty: “These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13).

The letter circles around three tests, again and again, like a spiral. The test of truth: do you confess that Jesus is the Christ who came in the flesh? The test of obedience: do you keep His commandments and walk as He walked? And the test of love: do you love your brothers and sisters? Those who claim to know God but fail these tests are deceived; those who pass them can be sure. Over everything stand two great statements about God: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5), and “God is love” (1 John 4:8).

The letter names no author, but from the earliest times the church has received it as the work of John the apostle, the son of Zebedee, the disciple whom Jesus loved. Its language and themes — light and darkness, truth and lies, life, love, remaining, being born of God — are unmistakably those of the Gospel of John. Tradition places John in Ephesus at the end of his long life, an old man among the churches of Asia, still repeating one message: love one another. The Son of Thunder (Mark 3:17) had become the apostle of love.

bridge.intro: 2 Peter ended by pointing ahead to 1 John and 2 John. Peter's last letter warned against false teachers and called believers to grow in the knowledge of Christ; John's first letter shows how to tell true knowledge from false, and true believers from false ones.

points.title: From Peter the Eyewitness to John the Eyewitness
points.body: Peter wrote, “we were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2 Peter 1:16). John begins in the same place, with what was heard, seen and touched (1 John 1:1). The two fishermen who ran together to the empty tomb both anchor the church in the same reality: the Son of God was not an idea or a vision, but a man of flesh and blood whom they knew.

points.title: From False Teachers to Antichrists
points.body: Peter warned, “as false teachers will also be among you” (2 Peter 2:1). John says they have arrived: “Little children, these are the end times, and as you heard that the Antichrist is coming, even now many antichrists have arisen” (1 John 2:18). Peter exposed their greed and immorality; John exposes their theology: they deny that Jesus is the Christ who has come in the flesh. And John gives the church tests to recognise them: “Beloved, don’t believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God” (1 John 4:1).

points.title: From ‘Grow in Knowledge’ to ‘That You May Know’
points.body: Peter's last words were, “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Peter 3:18). John's letter is about knowing: the word ‘know’ appears over thirty times. False teachers claimed secret knowledge; John says every believer knows God through Christ, and he gives clear signs by which they can know that they know Him (2:3). The goal is not mystery but assurance.

points.title: From ‘Beware’ to ‘Remain in Him’
points.body: Peter's final warning was, “beware, lest being carried away with the error of the wicked, you fall from your own steadfastness” (2 Peter 3:17). John's answer is one word repeated through the letter: μένω, remain, abide, continue. “Now, little children, remain in him, that when he appears, we may have boldness, and not be ashamed before him at his coming” (1 John 2:28). The defence against being carried away is staying close to Christ.

coreTheme.title: God Is Light, God Is Love — So That You May Know
paragraphs: John states the nature of God twice in the letter, and both statements shape everything. First: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5). God is pure, true and holy; those who claim fellowship with Him must walk in the light, confessing their sin rather than denying it. Second: “He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love” (1 John 4:8). God's very nature is self-giving love, shown supremely in the cross: “In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 4:10).

Because God is light, the believer's life must be marked by obedience and honesty about sin. Because God is love, the believer's life must be marked by love for others: “Beloved, let us love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God, and knows God” (1 John 4:7). Light and love are not two separate tests; they are two sides of knowing the same God.

And because God has revealed Himself in His Son, the believer can be sure. John's purpose statement comes near the end: “These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). His Gospel was written so that people might believe (John 20:31); his letter is written so that believers might know. Assurance is not arrogance; it is resting on God's own testimony about His Son (5:11–12).

These themes run through all of John's writings. The Gospel begins, “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1) and the letter begins, “That which was from the beginning” (1 John 1:1). Jesus gave the new commandment in the upper room: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another” (John 13:34). John, who leaned against Jesus' breast at that supper, spent the rest of his life repeating it.

truths.intro: As we journey through these 5 chapters, the Holy Spirit wants to anchor these truths in your spirit:

items.title: Jesus Really Came in the Flesh
items.body: The heart of the Christian faith is not an idea but a person who could be seen, heard and touched. “every spirit who confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God” (1 John 4:2). His real body, real blood and real death are the ground of forgiveness: “the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). Any teaching that makes Jesus less than fully God or less than fully human is not of God.

items.title: True Faith Shows in Obedience and Love
items.body: John will not allow a faith that only talks. “One who says, ‘I know him,’ and doesn’t keep his commandments, is a liar” (1 John 2:4), and “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18). Those who have been born of God will show it — imperfectly, but really — by turning from sin and loving others.

items.title: You Can Know You Have Eternal Life
items.body: God does not want His children to live in uncertainty. “He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life” (1 John 5:12). When you trust in Jesus, confess your sin, keep His word and love His people, you have the evidence of new birth. “We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

preparation.intro: Before we step into Chapter 1, prepare your spirit with these reflections:

items.title: Are You Sure?
items.body: Do you know that you have eternal life, or do you hope so, fear not, or simply never think about it? John writes so that you may know. As you read, ask the Holy Spirit to show you the evidence of His life in you — and to expose anything that is only talk.

items.title: Who Is Hard for You to Love?
items.body: John will say that whoever hates his brother is still in the darkness. Name the person in your church or family whom you find hardest to love. Bring that name to God before you begin, and read 1 John with that relationship open before Him.

prayerOfActivation: “Father, You are light, and in You is no darkness at all. You are love, and You showed Your love by sending Your Son as the atoning sacrifice for my sins. As I open the first letter of John, I thank You for the eyewitnesses who heard, saw and touched the Word of life, and for the eternal life that was with You and was revealed to us. Bring me into deeper fellowship with You and with Your Son, Jesus Christ. Where I walk in darkness, bring me into the light. Where I deny my sin, make me honest to confess it, and thank You that You are faithful and righteous to forgive me and cleanse me. Teach me to keep Your commandments and to walk as Jesus walked. Fill me with love for my brothers and sisters, in deed and in truth. Give me discernment to test the spirits and to hold to the truth that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. And let me know, with settled assurance, that I have eternal life in Your Son. In Jesus' name, Amen.”
